title: Module 3 assessment
subtitle: Formulas & Essential Functions
description: Fifteen questions across the whole of Module 3. Every question explains its answer, right or wrong.

questions.question: What does `=2+3*4` return?
questions.explanation: Multiplication runs before addition: 3x4 is 12, plus 2 is 14. Excel never warns you about precedence because the result is a valid number - which is exactly why brackets are worth writing even when optional.

questions.question: Rates sit across row 1 in B1:F1, quantities down column A in A2:A20. Write the formula for B2 that fills correctly across the whole grid.
questions.explanation: Column A is locked with the row free; row 1 is locked with the column free. This two-way grid pattern is the single most useful application of mixed references, and it is the difference between one formula and ninety-five.

questions.question: If six cells contain data and two of them hold a formula returning "", COUNTA returns 6 and COUNTBLANK returns 2.
questions.explanation: Both are right at once, which surprises people. COUNTA counts anything that is not truly empty, including a formula returning an empty string; COUNTBLANK also counts that empty string as blank. They are not complementary, and assuming they are produces totals that do not reconcile.

questions.question: `=ROUND(2.5,0)` and `=INT(2.5)` return what, in that order?
questions.explanation: ROUND goes to the nearest, with .5 going away from zero, so 3. INT simply discards the decimal part, so 2. On negatives they diverge further: INT(-2.5) is -3, because INT rounds down, not toward zero.

questions.question: Which formula totals sales for the North region only, with regions in A2:A100 and amounts in B2:B100?
questions.explanation: SUMIF takes the range to test first, then the criterion, then the range to add. SUMIFS reverses it - the sum range comes first. That inconsistency between the two functions is the most common cause of a wrong total in this family.

questions.question: You need to total amounts matching three conditions at once. SUMIF or SUMIFS?
options: SUMIF with the criteria joined by &
SUMIF repeated three times and added
SUMIFS - it takes multiple criteria pairs
questions.explanation: SUMIF handles exactly one condition. SUMIFS takes up to 127 criteria pairs and is the one to default to - using SUMIFS even for a single condition keeps the argument order consistent across your workbook.

questions.question: A commission rate used in forty formulas changes from 5% to 6%. The rate was typed into each formula. What went wrong, and what prevents it?
options: Nothing - updating forty formulas is normal
The rate should have been formatted as a percentage
Hard-coding. Put the rate in one named cell and reference it
questions.explanation: Any number appearing in more than one formula belongs in a labelled cell. A rate change then becomes one edit that cannot be applied partially - which is the real risk, because updating 29 of 40 produces a file that is quietly wrong rather than obviously broken.

questions.question: A defined name is absolute by default, so it does not shift when you copy the formula.
questions.explanation: Names behave like absolute references, which is most of their value - `=Price*TaxRate` reads like the business rule it encodes and survives copying. It also means a name is the wrong tool when you need the reference to move.

questions.question: Formula auditing - what does Trace Precedents show?
options: Which cells this one depends on
Which cells depend on this one
questions.explanation: Precedents feed in, dependents flow out. Trace Dependents is the one to run before deleting anything - it shows what will break, and it is how you avoid the #REF! that appears three sheets away.

questions.question: You select part of a formula in the Formula Bar and press F9. What happens?
options: The selected piece is replaced by its result, so you can see it
questions.explanation: F9 evaluates just the highlighted fragment, which is how you find which part of a long formula is misbehaving. Press Esc, not Enter, afterwards - Enter commits the substitution and destroys the formula.

questions.question: Write a formula that returns the largest value in B2:B50.
questions.explanation: MAX ignores text and blanks, so it is safe on a messy column. Pair it with MIN and AVERAGE for a three-formula sanity check on any new dataset - an impossible maximum usually means a stray entry or a units mistake.

questions.question: Pressing F9 while editing a reference cycles through the four locking combinations.
questions.explanation: F4 is the one that cycles A1, $A$1, A$1, $A1, then back. F9 evaluates the selected part of a formula instead. Press F4 repeatedly rather than typing dollar signs - it is faster and avoids the mis-typed `$A1$` that Excel rejects.

questions.question: `=COUNTIF(A2:A100,"*ltd*")` counts what?
options: Cells containing 'ltd' anywhere in the text
Nothing - COUNTIF does not take wildcards
questions.explanation: An asterisk stands for any run of characters, so this matches 'Acme Ltd' and 'Ltd Partners' alike. A question mark stands for exactly one character. Both work in COUNTIF, SUMIF and their IFS variants.

questions.question: A report has been quietly wrong for four months. Which habit would most likely have caught it?
options: Pressing Ctrl+` to show every formula and scanning for typed-over cells
questions.explanation: Ctrl+` reveals the whole sheet as formulas, and a cell holding a hard number where its neighbours hold formulas stands out immediately. That is the classic failure: someone typed over one formula to 'fix' a figure.

questions.question: Why does ROUND matter for currency when formatting already shows two decimals?
options: Formatting only hides the extra decimals, so totals can differ by a few paise from the displayed figures
questions.explanation: Twenty rows each hiding a third decimal can make a total that disagrees with the sum of what is on screen. Where the figure is money that someone will reconcile, round the value rather than the display.
